title: Mental distress and healthcare utilisation among sami and non-sami adults: a prospective registry-linked cohort study utilising data from the SAMINOR 2 questionnaire survey and the Norwegian control and payment of health reimbursements database (2012–2022)

paragraphs.en: According to the World Health Organisation [1], mental health conditions such as anxiety and depression are common across countries and communities. They are a leading contributor to disability and impose substantial costs on individuals, healthcare systems, and society. Mental distress is also profoundly linked to physical health in a bidirectional pathway. Depression and anxiety frequently coexist with chronic conditions such as cardiometabolic disease [2], diabetes [3], and chronic pain [4]. As a result, individuals experiencing mental distress often have more complex healthcare needs, making mental distress an important determinant of healthcare utilisation across both primary and specialist care settings.

Although mental health problems affect people globally, some groups face a disproportionately higher burden. Indigenous populations suffer from mental health challenges to a greater extent compared to non-Indigenous populations [5]. These mental health disparities are rooted in systemic marginalisation, discrimination and social exclusion stemming from the lasting impact of colonial practices and their intergenerational effects [6,7]. The interplay between historical and ongoing injustice, mental distress and somatic disorders, points towards an increased need for cultural appropriate healthcare services.

However, Indigenous populations generally experience significant disparities in the utilisation of health care services compared to non-Indigenous populations [8]. Also, Indigenous peoples have a lower use of non-emergency primary and specialised somatic healthcare services than that of non-Indigenous populations [9,10]. Instead, Indigenous individuals may tend to rely on emergency health care services [11,12].

The Sami are the Indigenous people of Sápmi, a region spanning northern Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Russia's Kola Peninsula. In Norway, the Indigenous Sami population has been subjected to long-standing structural discrimination through the official assimilation policy known as “Norwegianization,” which persisted until the mid-20th century [13]. Experiences of oppression and forced assimilation among Indigenous peoples, whether directly lived or passed down as generational colonial trauma, leads to health and socioeconomic disparities [14,15]. Comparative studies in Norway and Sweden have documented differences in mental distress and exposure to discrimination between the Sami and non-Sami population [16,17], as well as disparities in cardiometabolic health [18,19], with the Sami population exhibiting poorer outcomes. At the same time, it is important to acknowledge that the Norwegian context differs from many other Indigenous settings. Although disparities undoubtedly exist, differences in health, socioeconomic resources, and access to healthcare between Sami and non-Sami populations may be less pronounced than those documented for Indigenous populations in several other countries.

Still, barriers for use of health care among Sami mirror those reported for other Indigenous groups. The historical trauma leading to lack of trust in authority figures [13], and to communication challenges arising from linguistic and cultural differences between Sami patients and non-Sami health personnel [20], are likely to contribute to Sami refraining from use of health care services [21,22]. Strong cultural norms regarding privacy rendering open discussions of mental health inappropriate or stigmatised [23], may also impact on healthcare utilisation. While these cultural and structural factors are not measured in the present study, they provide an essential framework for interpreting potential differences in healthcare-seeking behaviour.

There is limited knowledge concerning Sami health and their use of healthcare services. In particular, little is known about whether Sami cultural and language background acts as an effect modifier of the association between high mental distress and healthcare service use compared with non-Sami populations.

The aim of this study was to investigate whether level of mental distress was associated with utilisation of primary and specialised healthcare services among Sami and non-Sami populations, and whether the impact of mental distress on healthcare utilisation differs between Sami and non-Sami.

For the current study, data from the SAMINOR 2 Questionnaire Survey was linked to data on healthcare utilisation retrieved from the Norwegian Control and Payment of Health Reimbursements database (KUHR-database) and demographic information from Statistics Norway (SSB) for the study period 2012–2022. Linkage was enabled through unique Norwegian personal identification numbers, which was replaced by project-specific identifiers by SSB to ensure participant confidentiality.

This was a prospective registry-linked cohort study, with follow up from 2012 to 2022 of an eligible sample of participants from the SAMINOR 2 Questionnaire Survey (hereafter referred to as SAMINOR 2). SAMINOR 2 was conducted in 2012 by the Centre for Sami Health Research, UiT The Arctic University of Norway as part of the second wave of the SAMINOR Study, a population-based study on health and living conditions in regions with Sami and Norwegian populations. A total of 11,600 individuals (27% of all invitees) from 25 municipalities participated (Figure 1). Further details on SAMINOR 2 have been published elsewhere [24]. The final sample in the current study was 10,517 individuals at baseline (2012): 5,832 women (1,418 Sami, 24.3%) and 4,685 men (1,085 Sami, 23.2%) Sample selection is outlined in Figure 2.

The primary outcome variables were the utilisation of primary healthcare (PHC) and specialist healthcare (SHC) during the period 2012–2022. The Norwegian health care system is universal and mainly tax founded, hereby levelling economic disparities through a redistribution of resources. All registered residents are entitled to a designated general practitioner (GP) through a list-based system designed to cover primary healthcare needs. GPs serve as gatekeepers to specialist healthcare and are responsible for referrals to specialist services, including specialist mental healthcare.

Data on health care utilisation was obtained from the KUHR-database, which records all patient contacts with publicly funded healthcare services through reimbursement claims submitted by healthcare providers. Each claim contains one or more diagnostic codes in accordance with the International Classification of Primary Care—2nd Edition (ICPC-2) or International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems 10th Revision (ICD-10) specifying the patient’s condition or reason for use of care. It also contains one or more codes specifying the type of care provided, in accordance with Norwegian regulations in effect at the time (Regulation of Medical Fees, 2003; Regulation of Outpatient Clinic Fees, 1992; Regulation of Psychologist Fees, 1997). In the current study, we excluded claims coded for procedures not involving direct contact between the patient and a medical doctor or psychologist (e.g. laboratory sample collection or diagnostic imaging typically performed by other health professionals), as well as claims related solely to administrative tasks or shift differentials. Remaining claims were categorised into two dependent variables according to the level of care defined by Norwegian legislation (The Health and Care Services Act, 2011; The Specialist Health Services Act, 1999): PHC, including services provided by general practitioners and community-based emergency care, and SHC, including specialists across all medical specialties, regional outpatient clinics, and psychologists. Both outcome variables were specified as the number of healthcare contacts for each individual during the period 2012–2022.

The main exposure variable was levels of mental distress, assessed by the Hopkins Symptoms Checklist with 10 items (HSCL-10). The HSCL-10 is a widely used patient-reported outcome tool measuring self-reported symptoms of anxiety and depression experienced during the last 4 weeks [25]. The anxiety dimension comprises items on sudden fear, feeling anxious, and faintness or dizziness, while the depression dimension comprises items on tension or upset, sadness or dejection, feelings of uselessness and self-blame, sleep problems, perceived struggle, and hopelessness. The checklist uses a 4-point scale (1: Not affected, 2: A little affected, 3: Quite a bit affected, 4: Extremely affected). Individuals with missing values on more than two items were excluded from the current study (Figure 2), and a person’s mean score was calculated by dividing the sums of scores by the number of items answered. A mean score ≥ 1.85 was used to indicate clinically relevant mental distress [25]. Lower scores do not imply absence of any psychological discomfort, but symptoms below the established clinical threshold. The main exposure variable was hence dichotomised: “high mental distress” indicates a score ≥ 1.85, and “low mental distress” indicates scores < 1.85.

Sami ethnicity was determined based on responses to 11 questionnaire items assessing self-identified ethnicity, ethnic background, and language affiliation. Participants could select one or more response options: Norwegian, Sami, Kven (a recognised national ethnic minority), or Other. For those selecting ‘Other,’ a free-text field was provided to specify ethnicity, ethnic background, or language affiliation. Individuals were defined as Sami if they answered ‘Sami’ to at least one of the two questions: ‘What do you consider yourself to be?’ or ‘What is your ethnic background?’. In addition, they needed to confirm at least one Sami language affiliation in response to the questions: ‘What language(s) do/did you, your parents, and your grandparents speak at home?’ The ethnicity variable was categorised into two categories: Sami (participants meeting the definition criteria), and non-Sami (all remaining participants). Participants whose ethnicity could not be determined because of missing data on the ethnicity-related items were excluded from the sample. We also excluded all participants defined to an ethnicity outside of the Nordic countries to reduce heterogeneity in the study sample (Figure 2).

Physical diseases were identified based on current or previous diagnoses of the following chronic conditions: diabetes, hypertension, angina, myocardial infarction, chronic bronchitis, asthma, eczema, psoriasis, multiple sclerosis, or Bechterew’s disease. Diagnoses were self-reported with the response options ‘Yes’ or ‘No’ to each condition separately. Chronic pain was assessed using a question consistent with the International Association for the Study of Pain (IASP) definition of chronic pain as pain lasting three months or longer [26]. Participants were asked: ‘During the past year, have you experienced pain or stiffness in muscles or bones lasting at least three months?’ Response options were ‘Yes’ or ‘No.’ To account for somatic health status, responses to chronic pain and chronic disease items were combined into a single binary variable labelled 'Chronic condition'. This was coded as 'yes' if the participant reported at least one of the listed diseases or chronic pain, and 'no' otherwise. Using this composite measure as an indicator of somatic health burden [27] allows the analysis to account for the total burden of morbidity, which is often a more relevant predictor of healthcare utilisation than specific diagnostic categories. Furthermore, this approach addresses the overlap often found between chronic diseases and chronic pain.

SAMINOR 2 participants were asked to give the total sum of all years of school and/or studies. Norwegian public education, including higher education, is tuition-free. While private alternatives exist, they play a limited role. We categorised the sums of years of education into two groups, roughly corresponding to the Norwegian education system in effect from the 1970s: Lower education (≤12 years - Primary and Secondary education), and Higher education (>12 years—University level).
To be included in SAMINOR 2, responders had to be between 18 and 69 years. Age was used as a continuous variable. Sex was used as a dichotomous variable with the options female or male.

Statistics Norway (SSB) is the national authority responsible for collecting, processing, and disseminating official statistics on the Norwegian population, economy, health, and education. SSB provided register-based information on emigration and death, including the month and year of any change in residency status. Each individual’s registered status was categorised as Living in Norway, Emigrated, or Deceased, with corresponding dates. Participants were censored from the analyses at the year and end of the month when they died or emigrated to indicate the end of each person’s time of possible observations. For each participant, the number of months within each calendar year any use of health care could be registered in KUHR was first calculated and follow-up time was subsequently converted to person-years (PYR) by dividing the total number of months by 12.

All analyses were stratified by sex. Descriptive characteristics are reported as frequency (percent) or mean (standard deviation (SD)). Pearson’s Chi-square test was used to compare distributions of categorical sample characteristics. Significant differences in mean age were assessed using the two-sample t-test.

In each subgroup of ethnicity and mental distress we calculated the total number of PHC and SHC consultations during the study period and the total person-years (PYR) of follow-up. Negative binomial regression models with a log link were used to examine the association between mental distress and PHC and SHC, using log-transformed person-years as an offset variable to account for varying follow-up time. Two models were fitted for each sex. Model 1 included age, ethnicity and mental distress as main effects along with a two-way interaction term ethnicity*mental distress, while Model 2 was additionally adjusted for length of education and the presence of chronic conditions. A complete case analysis approach was used, where individuals with missing data were excluded from the models in which those specific variables were included. Details regarding missing values are specified in the table footnotes.

From the models we estimated sex specific adjusted incidence rates with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) formed by the interaction ethnicity*mental distress. Adjusted incidence rate ratios with ‘no mental distress’ as reference were presented by ethnicity. Primary healthcare visits showed no evidence of substantial residual overdispersion, with Pearson chi-square/df ratios of 0.697 for women and 0.755 for men. In contrast, the specialist healthcare models showed some residual overdispersion (Pearson chi-square/df ratios of 1.428 for women and 1.411 for men). To account for this overdispersion and reduce the influence of high-utilisation observations in the specialist healthcare data, negative binomial regression models with robust standard errors were used. Residual diagnostics indicated that the models provided an adequate fit to the data. The level of statistical significance was set at 0.05 for all analyses. All analyses were done using IBM SPSS Statistics Version 31.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA).

The SAMINOR 2 Questionnaire Survey was conducted in 2012. The survey was approved by the Norwegian Data Protection Authority in 2011, and all participants gave informed consent to participate, including consent to link the SAMINOR data to national registers. For the current study, a Data Protection Impact Assessment was conducted by the Norwegian Agency for Shared Services in Education and Research (Sikt) in 2023 (741006/23) and approved by UiT The Artic University of Norway. Ethical approval was not deemed required by The Regional Committee for Medical and Health Research Ethics in Northern Norway (REK-Nord) (604937). A collective Sami consent was granted by The Ethical Committee for Sami Health Research in 2023 (23/3073-3). The SAMINOR Project Board approved the project in February 2024, and SAMINOR 2 and KUHR data were received in April 2024.

The study followed a baseline sample of 10,517 individuals from 2012-2022. Attrition due to emigrations and deaths was evenly distributed across sex and ethnic groups over the study period. Descriptive statistics for the variables included in the models are presented in Table 1. In both sexes, more Sami participants reported symptoms of mental distress above the cut-off score compared with non-Sami participants. Across all groups, high mental distress was consistently associated with lower education and the presence of chronic conditions. Sami individuals in both the high mental distress and low mental distress group reported having a chronic condition more frequently than non-Sami in the corresponding groups.

Altogether, the participants contributed 102,185 person-years of follow-up during the study period. A total of 840,246 PHC contacts and 230,538 SHC contacts were included (Table 2). Women contributed more healthcare contacts than men, and individuals with high mental distress had higher adjusted IRs of both PHC and SHC utilisation than those with low mental distress, regardless of ethnicity (Figure 3). Ethnic differences were generally small (Figure 3). Sami women showed slightly higher adjusted IRs for PHC and SHC use than non-Sami women at similar levels of mental distress. These patterns was also observed among men, except for PHC use in the low mental distress group, where Sami exhibited marginally lower adjusted IRs compared to non-Sami.

sections.title: Adjusted incidence rate ratios and observed interaction

paragraphs.en: Table 3 presents adjusted incidence rate ratios (adj. IRRs) for PHC and SHC utilisation (2012–2022) according to mental distress in Sami and non-Sami, stratified by sex. The reported p-values reflect the significance of the interaction term between ethnicity and mental distress. The interaction term was not statistically significant in either model for any of the groups across both types of care (Table 3). Mental distress was consistently associated with increased use of both PHC and SHC across sex and ethnicity. All lower IRR 95% confidence limits exceeded the reference value of 1, indicating statistically significant associations. An attenuation of the adj. IRR from Model 1 to the fully adjusted Model 2 was observed for all analyses.

In this large, register-linked cohort including Sami and non-Sami women and men in mid- and Northern Norway, high mental distress was consistently associated with higher rates of both primary and specialist healthcare utilisation. Overall, largely similar patterns of health care utilisation among Sami and non-Sami participants both in the low and high mental distress groups were observed. Sami women showed higher IRs for use of health care than non-Sami women in all analyses. The interaction analyses provided no evidence that the association between mental distress and use of health care differed by ethnicity in the fully adjusted model. Taken together, these findings suggest that ethnicity had little influence on the association between mental distress and use of health care and that the observed ethnic differences were largely explained by differences in the co-variates chronic conditions and length of education.

Both Sami women and Sami men reported higher levels of comorbidity than their non-Sami counterparts, regardless of level of mental distress. Based on health needs alone, consistently higher use of health care among Sami participants might therefore have been expected. The attenuation observed after adjustment for chronic conditions and length of education in Model 2 suggests that differences in health needs and socioeconomic resources partly accounted for the observed patterns. Of these factors, chronic conditions are likely to be particularly important, as they directly reflect healthcare needs.

Length of education may nevertheless also have contributed to the differences observed in the crude analyses. Participants with high mental distress generally had lower educational attainment than those with low mental distress, whereas Sami women were more likely than any other group to have more than 12 years of education. Educational attainment is a well-established social determinant of health and has been associated with lower mortality rates [28], possibly driven through improved health literacy and a greater ability to access and navigate healthcare services. Together with the higher burden of certain chronic conditions, cardiovascular risk factors, and mental distress reported in previous SAMINOR studies [16,18,29], these factors may help explain part of the ethnic differences observed in the unadjusted analyses. However, as these variables were included in the adjusted models, the remaining differences in healthcare use are likely to reflect additional factors beyond measured health needs and educational attainment.

Our findings suggest that healthcare utilisation rates may not fully reflect underlying healthcare needs, especially among men, and that individuals reporting similar levels of mental distress may differ in when and under what circumstances they seek healthcare. Rosic et al [30]. found that Sami patients with psoriatic arthritis experienced longer symptom duration before receiving a diagnosis than non-Sami patients. Although their findings cannot be directly transferred to the present study, they suggest that healthcare contact may occur later in the development of disease among some Sami patients. If healthcare is sought at a later stage of illness, when symptoms are more advanced, a higher number of consultations may be required to manage the condition and monitor recovery.

Utilisation rates alone should therefore not necessarily be interpreted as reflecting similar symptom-severity or healthcare needs at the time of contact. The observed healthcare utilisation rates in the current study could indicate an ethnicity-related higher threshold for seeking care, a pattern consistent with findings from Indigenous populations internationally. A systematic review from Canada, Australia and other Indigenous settings showed that Indigenous populations often experience a greater burden of illness while underutilising healthcare services relative to their health needs [9]. Several factors may contribute to ethnic differences in help-seeking behaviour. In Sami culture, particularly among older generations, acknowledging illness or mental health difficulties has been described as inconsistent with values emphasising endurance, self-reliance, and resilience [31]. Similarly, research suggests that Sami children are often raised to develop hardiness through encouragement of independence and autonomy from an early age. The concept of hardiness is most closely associated having the skills, knowledge, and mental strength to take care of oneself and others [32,33]. Such values may influence both symptom interpretation and the threshold for seeking healthcare. In addition, mental health problems may be more stigmatised in some Sami communities, and traditional healing practices may also influence healthcare-seeking patterns [34], although these practices generally complement rather than replace conventional healthcare [35].

Differences in healthcare access may provide an additional explanation. Ethnic differences were generally smaller for specialist healthcare than for primary healthcare, possibly reflecting the organisation of the Norwegian healthcare system, where primary healthcare providers act as gatekeepers to specialist services. Thus, variations in help-seeking behaviour are more likely to influence primary healthcare use than specialist healthcare use. Our findings do not indicate reduced access to specialist healthcare among Sami participants once contact with primary healthcare has been established.

Healthcare utilisation has previously been reported to be higher in Northern Norway than in southern regions of the country, despite longer travel distances and fewer healthcare resources [36,37]. Unlike many Indigenous populations internationally, the Sami and non-Sami populations in Northern Norway often live in the same communities, share healthcare services, and are embedded within similar social and geographic contexts. This close proximity may contribute to more similar patterns of healthcare utilisation than those observed in other studies comparing an Indigenous population to a non-Indigenous benchmark population. Nevertheless, culturally specific factors may still influence healthcare experiences and preferences. For example, Sami individuals in Sweden have reported travelling considerable distances to access culturally adapted mental health services in Norway rather than using geographically closer services that were perceived as less culturally appropriate [38]. This suggests that even where overall patterns of healthcare utilisation are similar, access to culturally safe and culturally adapted services may remain important for Sami service users.

Our findings provide limited support for ethnic differences in the association between mental distress and use of health care when comparing Sami and non-Sami. Similar levels of healthcare use may not necessarily reflect similar levels of need, symptom burden, or healthcare access. As such, the findings raise important questions about how healthcare utilisation rates should be interpreted in studies including Indigenous individuals. It is important to acknowledge that disparities between Sami and non-Sami populations in Norway may be less pronounced than those reported for many Indigenous populations elsewhere, particularly regarding disease burden, socioeconomic conditions, and access to healthcare.

To our knowledge, this is one of the first studies to examine whether the association between mental distress and the use of primary and specialised healthcare services differs between Sami and non-Sami populations in northern Norway. As Sami ethnicity is not recorded in national health registers, the SAMINOR Study provides a unique opportunity to compare Sami and non-Sami populations through its uniquely comprehensive mapping of ethnicity. Furthermore, the large sample size, drawn from multiple municipalities, ensures a robust representation of Sami settlement areas in Northern Norway.

Another major strength in this study lies in its use of the national KUHR database, which includes all reimbursement claims from primary healthcare providers. This ensures that the database offers a reliable and accurate account of the actual number of consultations in primary and specialist services, free of recollection bias. By integrating these datasets, the study provides a unique opportunity to investigate factors that would otherwise remain inaccessible.

The use of the HSCL-10 tool for quantifying symptoms of mental distress also adds to the validity of the results in this study. In a scoping review looking at tools for depression screening in Indigenous population, several studies found standard mental health screening tools to be inappropriate because of the different cultural views of mental health [39]. Differences in language, cultural norms, and the origin and handling of mental distress may influence both how symptoms are experienced and how individuals respond to questionnaire items. However, the HSCL-10 instrument has shown no variance in capturing mental distress in Sami and non-Sami SAMINOR 2 study participants [40].

Mental distress was measured only at baseline. Changes in mental health status during the follow-up period were not captured, and some participants may have developed or recovered from mental distress during the period of follow-up. This lack of repeated measures likely leads to non-differential misclassification of the exposure over time. Such misclassification typically results in regression dilution bias, as the baseline status becomes less representative of the actual exposure as time progresses [41]. Consequently, the true relationship between mental distress and healthcare utilisation may be stronger than what is reported in this study. While the large sample size is a notable strength, he 27% response may limit the generalisability of the findings. Low response rates can lead to selection bias if participants differ systematically from non-participants regarding characteristics relevant to the study. If non-participants have a higher or lower burden of mental distress or different patterns of healthcare utilisation, our findings may underestimate the true associations. However, while low response rates significantly affect prevalence estimates, the associations between variables (such as the incidence rate ratios reported here) tend to be more robust against selection bias [41]. Therefore, the study sample may not fully reflect the broader Sami and non-Sami populations, and the findings should therefore be interpreted with some caution.

Furthermore, the size of the Sami population remains uncertain, primarily because ethnicity is not recorded in national population or health registers in Norway. Consequently, it is not possible to determine whether participation rates differ between Sami and non-Sami individuals, which may have introduced selection bias into the study. While the SAMINOR 2 Survey provides a unique opportunity to identify Sami participants through self-reported ethnic affiliation, some degree of misclassification bias may be present. Ethnic identity is complex and multidimensional, and different operationalizations of Sami ethnicity may classify individuals differently. Therefore, the observed results may have varied had another definition of ethnicity been applied. If present, such misclassification would likely underestimate potential ethnic differences in healthcare utilisation differences between Sami and non-Sami participants.

Healthcare utilisation was measured as contact counts, which do not capture the quality, appropriateness, or effectiveness of the care received. This measure also fails to identify unmet needs, like in instances where individuals may have required care but did not seek or receive it. Furthermore, because the assessment of mental distress and chronic illness relied on a limited set of self-reported variables, the possibility of residual confounding cannot be ruled out. This limits our capacity to fully evaluate the clinical adequacy of the healthcare utilisation and should be kept in mind when interpreting the results.

This study demonstrates that mental distress is associated with increased utilisation of both primary and specialist healthcare services among Sami and non-Sami populations, with only modest ethnic differences. While these findings suggest broadly comparable access to healthcare services, utilisation rates alone cannot fully capture differences in healthcare-seeking behaviour, care pathways, or experiences of care. Also, common living conditions, universal healthcare coverage, and longstanding cultural exchange between Sami and non-Sami populations may have contributed to converging patterns of healthcare utilisation in northern Norway. This may partly explain why the ethnic differences observed in the present study were smaller than those reported among Indigenous populations in other national contexts. Future studies should therefore move beyond measures of service use to examine how cultural, structural, and contextual factors shape engagement with healthcare among Sami and non-Sami populations.
